title: The Thousand Brains Theory
intro: Jeff Hawkins and colleagues at Numenta propose that every cortical column learns complete models of objects, not just fragments of them, by pairing what it senses with where its sensor is in the object's own reference frame. Thousands of columns model the same object in parallel and vote to agree on what it is.

blocks.text: The classic view of the cortex is a hierarchy: low regions detect edges, higher regions combine them, and only at the top does a whole object get recognised. The Thousand Brains Theory keeps the hierarchy but changes what each level does. It claims every column, even in primary sensory cortex, is a complete sensorimotor modelling system. A column receiving input from a patch of fingertip learns the shape of a coffee cup by moving that fingertip around the cup and noting which feature it feels at which location on the cup. Many columns, attached to different patches of skin or retina, learn models of the same cup. Recognition is then a consensus among a thousand small brains rather than the output of one top-level detector.

Close your eyes and run a finger over a coffee mug. Each touch gives you a small patch of sensation — a curved surface, an edge, the handle — and yet after two or three touches you know it is a mug. Grab it with your whole hand and you may recognise it at once. The Thousand Brains Theory explains both observations with one idea: each patch of sensor feeds a cortical column that knows where on the object it is touching, so each column can learn and recognise whole objects as arrangements of features at locations. One column needs several movements to narrow down the possibilities; many columns touching different places at once can share their guesses and agree in a single step.

This builds directly on Hierarchical Temporal Memory (#/brain/computational-cortical-columns/htm). In HTM's temporal memory, distal dendritic segments let a cell predict its next input from the sequence context. In the Thousand Brains Theory the same mechanism predicts the next input from a location context instead: if I am at this location on this object, I expect this feature. Hawkins, Ahmad & Cui (2017) introduced the column model with an allocentric location signal; Lewis et al. (2019) proposed that the location signal comes from grid-cell-like modules in the cortex; Hawkins et al. (2019) and the book A Thousand Brains (Hawkins 2021) set out the full framework. Since 2024 the open-source Thousand Brains Project has been building a sensorimotor learning system, Monty, on these principles.

items: Reference frames: each column keeps a representation of location relative to the object being sensed, not relative to the body. A location on the cup's handle is the same location wherever the cup sits on the table.

Movement updates location: when the sensor moves, the column updates its location estimate by path integration, the way grid cells in the entorhinal cortex update an animal's position as it walks. The theory proposes that cortical columns contain grid-cell-like cells, probably in L6 (see #/brain/neuroscience/cortical-columns/reference-frames).

Features at locations: a layer, proposed to be L4, combines the sensed feature with the current location, so the column learns objects as sets of feature-at-location pairs. This layer uses the same dendritic sequence machinery as temporal memory, with location in place of the previous input as context (see #/brain/neuroscience/cortical-columns/temporal-memory).

Voting: an object layer, proposed to be L2/3, holds a stable representation of the object being sensed. Long-range lateral connections between object layers of different columns let each column narrow its candidates using the others' evidence.

blocks.text: How recognition works, step by step

Suppose your fingertip touches something smooth and curved. Many objects have a smooth curved region somewhere, so the column's object layer activates a union of candidate objects (a cup, a bowl, a ball), each paired with the locations on it where such a feature could be. You move the finger 2 cm up. The column shifts every candidate location by that movement and predicts what it should feel next under each hypothesis. The next touch is a rim, which only the cup and bowl predict there, so the ball drops out. After a few touches a single object remains. One column needs several movements to get there. Several fingers touching at once can share evidence through voting and often recognise the object in one grasp, which is what the simulation below shows.

Each object is ten locations, each holding one of a small set of features. On every step each column touches a random location on the true object and keeps only the objects consistent with everything it has felt so far. The first curve is one column on its own. The second is several columns whose candidate sets are intersected after every step, the role of lateral voting. Try it: with three columns the candidates collapse after one or two sensations, while one column needs many. Raise the number of objects, or lower the number of distinct features, and recognition gets harder for both, since more objects share features at the same locations. The simplified sim assumes each column already knows its location on the object; in the real theory that location must itself be inferred, which is one of the harder parts of the model.

This plot reproduces, in miniature, the main result in Hawkins, Ahmad and Cui (2017): with lateral voting, the number of sensations needed to recognise an object drops sharply as the number of columns grows.

blocks.alt: A mug drawn at the top with three numbered contact points: 1 on the rim, 2 on the side and 3 on the handle. Dotted arrows lead from each point to one of three boxes, Column 1, Column 2 and Column 3. Each box lists what its column could be sensing: column 1 mug, bowl or can; column 2 mug, can or vase; column 3 mug, jug or teapot. Mug is highlighted in blue in every box and the other candidates are struck through. Purple double-headed arrows join the boxes to each other, labelled long-range lateral connections in L2/3 carry each column's hypotheses. A blue banner at the bottom reads: only mug fits all three, every column settles on it.
blocks.caption: Why more columns need fewer touches: each column keeps every object consistent with its own patch, and lateral voting leaves only the object they all agree on. In the theory this sharing runs over long-range connections in L2/3; that those connections carry votes is a proposal, not an observation.

blocks.text: Real objects are made of other objects: a cup with a logo, a car with wheels. The 2019 framework paper proposes displacement cells, which represent the relative position of two locations in two reference frames, such as where the logo's reference frame sits within the cup's. Displacement cells would let a column learn compositional structure and also represent movement itself: the displacement between the current and the next location is exactly the motor command needed to get there. This part of the theory is the most speculative and has the least direct evidence.
What fits the evidence, and what is open

items: Supported: cortex is broadly uniform; every region has L5 motor-related output; columns in primary sensory areas respond to some object-level and context-level properties; grid cells exist in entorhinal cortex, and grid-like coding has been reported in human cortex during navigation and conceptual tasks with fMRI.
Plausible but not shown: that L6 holds grid-cell modules for each column, and that L4 learns features at locations.

Open: how reference frames are anchored and re-anchored, how displacement cells would work, how the theory scales to abstract concepts and language, and how well it competes with deep learning on real tasks. Numenta's Monty project is an open-source implementation testing these ideas.

blocks.text: Why it matters for building a mini brain

For a builder the theory is attractive because it implies the same column, copied many times, can learn anything given the right sensors and movement signals. It also gives a concrete wiring diagram: an input layer combining sensation with location, a location layer doing path integration, and an object layer with lateral connections for voting. Building a Column from Spiking Neurons (#/brain/neuroscience/cortical-columns/column-blueprint) turns that diagram into a staged plan.

The theory also tells you what extra machinery a column needs beyond a sequence memory: a location signal driven by movement (path integration), a way to associate sensed features with locations (dendritic segments in the sensory layer), and lateral connections between columns that represent each column's current set of candidate objects. Each of these has a plausible spiking implementation — continuous attractor networks or oscillatory phase codes for grid-like locations, NMDA-like dendritic subunits for feature-location association, and excitatory lateral connections plus inhibition for voting. The Thousand Brains pages of the Computational Cortical Columns path (#/brain/computational-cortical-columns/thousand-brains) sketch each of these, and its Step-by-Step Roadmap (#/brain/computational-cortical-columns/building-an-snn-column/roadmap) puts them in build order.

items: Each column learns complete object models, not just fragments that are assembled higher up a hierarchy.
Objects are stored as features at locations in object-centric reference frames; the location signal is updated by movement.
A single column recognises objects by integrating several sensations over movements; many columns can recognise in one step by voting.
The anatomical mapping (L4 features, L6 locations, L2/3 voting) is a hypothesis, not an established fact.
Monty is the reference implementation to read and run before building your own spiking version.

blocks.text: The Computational Cortical Columns path takes each piece of the theory further, in this order:

items: Reference Frames (#/brain/computational-cortical-columns/thousand-brains/reference-frames) — why the theory puts location at the centre: objects stored as features at locations in object-centric reference frames, and why that helps generalisation and compositional structure.

Grid and Displacement Cells (#/brain/computational-cortical-columns/thousand-brains/grid-and-displacement-cells) — grid cells, path integration, and the proposal that cortical columns use grid-cell-like modules to encode locations on objects, plus hypothetical displacement cells for relations between objects.

Sensorimotor Object Recognition (#/brain/computational-cortical-columns/thousand-brains/sensorimotor-object-recognition) — recognising an object by moving a sensor over it: feature-location pairs, a shrinking set of candidate objects, and how movement drives inference. Interactive: a single column needing several sensations.

Voting Between Columns (#/brain/computational-cortical-columns/thousand-brains/column-voting) — how columns that sense different parts of an object reach consensus through lateral connections, and why that allows recognition in one glance. Interactive: multi-column voting with a sensations-versus-columns curve.

Monty and the Thousand Brains Project (#/brain/computational-cortical-columns/thousand-brains/monty) — the open-source implementation: sensor modules, learning modules, the Cortical Messaging Protocol, and how to experiment with it.
